title: Book 8, Chapter 24 — Nineteenth and Twentieth Years of the War—Revolt of Ionia— Intervention of Persia—The War in Ionia
paragraphs: When the news reached Athens, the Athenians refused for a long while to believe it, even from the most respectable of the soldiers who had escaped from the scene themselves and reported it plainly. A destruction so complete did not seem credible. When they were forced to accept it, they turned in anger on the orators who had helped to promote the expedition, as if they had not voted for it themselves. They were enraged also with the reciters of oracles, the soothsayers and all the other omen-mongers of the time who had encouraged them to hope that they would conquer Sicily. They were already distressed at every point and in every quarter, and after this blow they were seized by a fear and consternation without example. It was grievous enough for the state, and for every man in his own person, to lose so many heavy infantry, cavalry and able-bodied troops, and to see none left to replace them. But they also saw that they did not have enough ships in the docks, or money in the treasury, or crews for the ships, and they began to despair of safety. They thought that their enemies in Sicily, inflamed by so signal a victory, would sail at once with their fleet against Piraeus. They thought that their adversaries at home would redouble all their preparations and attack them vigorously by sea and land together, helped by their own revolted allies. Nevertheless, with the means they had, they determined to resist to the last. They resolved to provide timber and money, to equip a fleet as best they could, and to take steps to secure their allies, above all Euboea. They resolved to reform the city’s affairs on a more economical footing, and to elect a board of elders to advise on the state of affairs as occasion required. In short, as is the way of a democracy, in the panic of the moment they were ready to be as prudent as possible.

These resolutions were carried out at once. Summer was now over. In the winter that followed, all Hellas was stirred by the great Athenian disaster in Sicily. Neutrals felt that even without an invitation they could no longer stand aloof from the war, and that they ought to volunteer to march against the Athenians. Each of them reflected that the Athenians would probably have come against them if the Sicilian campaign had succeeded. They also considered that the war would now be short, and that it would be creditable to take part in it. Meanwhile the allies of the Lacedaemonians were more anxious than ever to see a speedy end to their heavy labors. But above all, the subjects of the Athenians showed a readiness to revolt even beyond their ability. They judged the circumstances with passion, and would not even hear that the Athenians could last out the coming summer. Besides all this, Lacedaemon was encouraged by the near prospect of being joined in great force in the spring by her allies in Sicily, who had lately been forced by events to acquire a navy. With these reasons for confidence in every quarter, the Lacedaemonians resolved to throw themselves into the war without reserve. They considered that once it was happily ended, they would be finally delivered from dangers like the one that would have threatened them from Athens had she become mistress of Sicily, and that the overthrow of the Athenians would leave them in quiet enjoyment of the supremacy over all Hellas.

Their king, Agis, therefore set out at once that winter with some troops from Decelea. He levied contributions for the fleet from the allies. Turning toward the Malian Gulf, he exacted a sum of money from the Oetaeans by carrying off most of their cattle, in reprisal for their old hostility. In spite of the protests and opposition of the Thessalians, he forced the Achaeans of Phthiotis and the other subjects of the Thessalians in those parts to give him money and hostages. He deposited the hostages at Corinth and tried to bring their countrymen into the confederacy. The Lacedaemonians now sent a requisition to the cities for the building of a hundred ships. They fixed their own quota and that of the Boeotians at twenty-five each; that of the Phocians and Locrians together at fifteen; that of the Corinthians at fifteen; that of the Arcadians, Pellenians and Sicyonians together at ten; and that of the Megarians, Troezenians, Epidaurians and Hermionians together at ten also. Meanwhile they made every other preparation to begin hostilities by the spring.

In the meantime the Athenians were not idle. During this same winter they did as they had determined: they contributed timber and pushed on their shipbuilding. They fortified Sunium so that their corn-ships could round it in safety, and they evacuated the fort in Laconia that they had built on their way to Sicily. For the sake of economy they also cut down any other expenses that seemed unnecessary, and above all they kept a careful lookout against the revolt of their allies.

While both sides were thus engaged, and were as intent on preparing for the war as they had been at the outset, the Euboeans were the first to act. During this winter they sent envoys to Agis to treat about revolting from Athens. Agis accepted their proposals and sent for Alcamenes, son of Sthenelaidas, and Melanthus from Lacedaemon to take command in Euboea. These arrived with some three hundred Neodamodes, and Agis began to arrange for their crossing. But in the meanwhile some Lesbians arrived who also wished to revolt. They were supported by the Boeotians, and Agis was persuaded to put off acting in the matter of Euboea. He made arrangements for the revolt of the Lesbians, giving them Alcamenes, who was to have sailed to Euboea, as governor. He himself promised them ten ships, and the Boeotians promised the same number. All this was done without instructions from home. While Agis was at Decelea with the army he commanded, he had power to send troops wherever he pleased and to levy men and money. During this period, one might say, the allies obeyed him much more than they obeyed the Lacedaemonians in the city, since the force he had with him made him feared at once wherever he went. While Agis was occupied with the Lesbians, the Chians and Erythraeans, who were also ready to revolt, applied not to him but at Lacedaemon. They arrived accompanied by an ambassador from Tissaphernes, the commander of King Darius, son of Artaxerxes, in the maritime districts. He invited the Peloponnesians to come over, and promised to maintain their army. The King had recently called on him for the tribute from his government, which was in arrears because he had been unable to raise it from the Hellenic towns on account of the Athenians. He therefore calculated that by weakening the Athenians he would get the tribute better paid, and that he would also draw the Lacedaemonians into alliance with the King. By this means, as the King had commanded him, he would take Amorges alive or dead. Amorges was the bastard son of Pissuthnes, and was in rebellion on the coast of Caria.

While the Chians and Tissaphernes were thus joining to effect the same object, at about the same time Calligeitus, son of Laophon, a Megarian, and Timagoras, son of Athenagoras, a Cyzicene, arrived at Lacedaemon. Both were exiles from their countries and living at the court of Pharnabazus, son of Pharnaces, and they came on a mission from Pharnabazus to procure a fleet for the Hellespont. By means of it, if possible, he hoped to achieve the very object of Tissaphernes’ ambition himself: to cause the cities in his government to revolt from the Athenians, to get the tribute, and to win the alliance of the Lacedaemonians for the King through his own agency.

The emissaries of Pharnabazus and Tissaphernes negotiated separately, and a keen competition now arose at Lacedaemon over whether a fleet and army should be sent first to Ionia and Chios, or to the Hellespont. The Lacedaemonians, however, decidedly favored the Chians and Tissaphernes, who were backed by Alcibiades, the family friend of Endius, one of the ephors for that year. Indeed, this is how their house got its Laconic name: Alcibiades was the family name of Endius. Nevertheless the Lacedaemonians first sent Phrynis, one of the Perioeci, to Chios, to see whether the Chians had as many ships as they said and whether their city was generally as great as reported. When he brought word that they had been told the truth, the Lacedaemonians immediately made an alliance with the Chians and Erythraeans and voted to send them forty ships. According to the Chians, there were already not less than sixty in the island. At first the Lacedaemonians meant to send ten of these forty themselves, with Melanchridas as their admiral. But afterwards an earthquake occurred, and they sent Chalcideus instead of Melanchridas, and equipped only five ships in Laconia instead of ten. And the winter ended, and with it ended the nineteenth year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.

At the beginning of the next summer the Chians urged that the fleet be sent off. They were afraid that the Athenians, from whom all these embassies were kept secret, might find out what was going on. The Lacedaemonians at once sent three Spartans to Corinth to haul the ships across the Isthmus as quickly as possible, from the sea on one side to the sea on the side of Athens, and to order them all to sail to Chios, including those that Agis was equipping for Lesbos. The number of ships from the allied states was thirty-nine in all.

Meanwhile Calligeitus and Timagoras, on behalf of Pharnabazus, did not join the expedition to Chios, and did not give the money they had brought with them to help in dispatching a force, twenty-five talents. They determined instead to sail later by themselves with another force. Agis, for his part, saw that the Lacedaemonians were bent on going to Chios first, and came around to their view himself. The allies assembled at Corinth and held a council. They decided to sail first to Chios under the command of Chalcideus, who was equipping the five vessels in Laconia; then to Lesbos, under the command of Alcamenes, the man Agis had already chosen; and lastly to go to the Hellespont, where the command was given to Clearchus, son of Ramphias. They would take only half the ships across the Isthmus first and let those sail off at once. Their purpose was that the Athenians should attend less to the departing squadron than to the ships to be taken across afterwards. No care had been taken to keep this voyage secret, out of contempt for the impotence of the Athenians, who as yet had no fleet of any account on the sea. In accordance with this decision, twenty-one vessels were at once conveyed across the Isthmus.

They were now impatient to set sail, but the Corinthians were unwilling to accompany them until they had celebrated the Isthmian festival, which fell at that time. Agis proposed to spare them their scruples about breaking the Isthmian truce by taking the expedition on himself. The Corinthians would not consent to this, and a delay followed. During it the Athenians began to suspect what was being prepared at Chios. They sent Aristocrates, one of their generals, who charged the Chians with it. When the Chians denied it, he ordered them to send a contingent of ships with him, as faithful allies. Seven were sent. The reason for sending the ships lay in the fact that the mass of the Chians were not privy to the negotiations. The few who were in the secret did not wish to break with the multitude until they had something definite to lean on, and since the Peloponnesians were delayed, they no longer expected them to arrive.

In the meantime the Isthmian games took place, and the Athenians, who had also been invited, went to attend them. They now saw more clearly into the designs of the Chians, and as soon as they returned to Athens they took measures to prevent the fleet from putting out from Cenchreae without their knowledge. After the festival the Peloponnesians set sail for Chios with twenty-one ships under the command of Alcamenes. The Athenians first sailed against them with an equal number, drawing off toward the open sea. But the enemy turned back before he had followed them far, and the Athenians returned too, since they did not trust the seven Chian ships that formed part of their number. They afterwards manned thirty-seven vessels in all and chased the enemy along the coast into Spiraeum, a desert Corinthian port on the edge of the Epidaurian frontier. The Peloponnesians lost one ship out at sea, then got the rest together and brought them to anchor. The Athenians now attacked not only from the sea with their fleet but also disembarked on the coast. A melee followed of the most confused and violent kind, in which the Athenians disabled most of the enemy’s vessels and killed Alcamenes their commander, losing also a few of their own men.

After this they separated. The Athenians detached enough ships to blockade those of the enemy and anchored with the rest at the adjacent islet, where they proceeded to encamp, and they sent to Athens for reinforcements. On the day after the battle the Peloponnesians had been joined by the Corinthians, who came to help the ships, and not long afterwards by the other inhabitants of the vicinity. These saw how hard it was to keep guard in a desert place. In their perplexity they first thought of burning the ships, but finally resolved to haul them up on shore and sit down and guard them with their land forces until a convenient opportunity of escape should present itself. Agis, on being informed of the disaster, also sent them a Spartan named Thermon. The Lacedaemonians had first received the news that the fleet had put out from the Isthmus, since the ephors had ordered Alcamenes to send off a horseman when this happened. They immediately resolved to dispatch their own five vessels under Chalcideus, and Alcibiades with him. But while they were full of this resolution, the second news came that the fleet had taken refuge in Spiraeum. They were disheartened that their first step in the Ionian war had failed, and they gave up the idea of sending the ships from their own country, and even wished to recall some that had already sailed.

Perceiving this, Alcibiades again persuaded Endius and the other ephors to persevere in the expedition. He said that the voyage would be made before the Chians heard of the fleet’s misfortune, and that as soon as he set foot in Ionia he would have no difficulty in persuading the cities to revolt, by assuring them of the weakness of the Athenians and the zeal of Lacedaemon, since they would readily believe his testimony. He also represented to Endius himself in private that it would be glorious for him to be the means of making Ionia revolt and the King become the ally of Lacedaemon, instead of leaving that honor to Agis (Agis, it must be remembered, was the enemy of Alcibiades). Endius and his colleagues were thus persuaded, and Alcibiades put to sea with the five ships and the Lacedaemonian Chalcideus, and made all haste on the voyage.

About this time the sixteen Peloponnesian ships from Sicily, which had served through the war with Gylippus, were caught off Leucadia on their return. The twenty-seven Athenian vessels under Hippocles, son of Menippus, which were on the lookout for the ships from Sicily, handled them roughly. After losing one of their number, the rest escaped from the Athenians and sailed into Corinth.

Meanwhile Chalcideus and Alcibiades seized everyone they met on their voyage, to prevent news of their coming, and let them go at Corycus, the first point on the continent where they touched. There they were visited by some of their Chian correspondents. Urged by them to sail up to the town without announcing their coming, they arrived suddenly before Chios. The many were amazed and confounded, while the few had arranged for the council to be sitting at that time. Chalcideus and Alcibiades made speeches stating that many more ships were sailing up, but said nothing of the fleet being blockaded in Spiraeum. After this the Chians revolted from the Athenians, and the Erythraeans immediately afterwards. Then three vessels sailed over to Clazomenae and made that city revolt too. The Clazomenians at once crossed over to the mainland and began to fortify Polichna, so that they could retreat there, if necessary, from the island where they lived.

While the revolted places were all engaged in fortifying and preparing for the war, news of Chios speedily reached Athens. The Athenians thought the danger now menacing them great and unmistakable. They thought that the rest of their allies would not consent to keep quiet after the secession of the greatest of their number. In the consternation of the moment they at once took off the penalty attaching to anyone who proposed or put to the vote a proposal to use the thousand talents. They had jealously avoided touching these throughout the whole war. They voted to employ them to man a large number of ships. They voted also to send off at once, under Strombichides, son of Diotimus, the eight vessels from the blockading fleet at Spiraeum that had left the blockade and returned after pursuing the vessels with Chalcideus and failing to overtake them. Twelve more under Thrasycles, also taken from the blockade, were to follow shortly afterwards. They also recalled the seven Chian vessels that formed part of their squadron blockading the fleet in Spiraeum. They gave the slaves on board their liberty and put the freemen in confinement. They speedily manned and sent out ten fresh ships to blockade the Peloponnesians in place of all those that had departed, and decided to man thirty more. Zeal was not lacking, and no effort was spared to send relief to Chios.

In the meantime Strombichides with his eight ships arrived at Samos and, taking one Samian vessel, sailed to Teos and required the Teians to remain quiet. Chalcideus also set sail from Chios for Teos with twenty-three ships, while the land forces of the Clazomenians and Erythraeans moved along the coast to support him. Strombichides was informed of this in time and put out from Teos before they arrived. While out at sea he saw the number of the ships from Chios and fled toward Samos, with the enemy chasing him. The Teians at first would not receive the land forces, but when the Athenians fled they took them into the town. There the land forces waited some time for Chalcideus to return from the pursuit. As time passed without his appearing, they began to demolish the wall that the Athenians had built on the land side of the city of the Teians. They were helped by a few of the barbarians who had come up under the command of Stages, the lieutenant of Tissaphernes.

Meanwhile Chalcideus and Alcibiades had chased Strombichides into Samos. They armed the crews of the ships from Peloponnese and left them at Chios, filled their places with substitutes from Chios, manned twenty other ships, and sailed off to bring about the revolt of Miletus. Alcibiades, who had friends among the leading men of the Milesians, wished to bring over the town before the ships from Peloponnese arrived. By causing the revolt of as many cities as possible with the help of the Chian power and of Chalcideus, he meant to secure the honor for the Chians, for himself and Chalcideus, and, as he had promised, for Endius, who had sent them out. They were not discovered until their voyage was nearly completed, and they arrived a little before Strombichides and Thrasycles. (Thrasycles had just come from Athens with twelve ships and had joined Strombichides in pursuing them.) They brought about the revolt of Miletus. The Athenians, sailing up close on their heels with nineteen ships, found Miletus closed against them and took up their station at the adjacent island of Lade. The first alliance between the King and the Lacedaemonians was concluded by Tissaphernes and Chalcideus immediately after the revolt of the Milesians, and was as follows:
The Lacedaemonians and their allies made a treaty with the King and Tissaphernes on the following terms:

1. Whatever country or cities the King has, or the King’s ancestors had, shall be the king’s. And whatever came in to the Athenians from these cities, whether money or anything else, the King and the Lacedaemonians and their allies shall jointly prevent the Athenians from receiving, whether money or anything else.

2. The war with the Athenians shall be carried on jointly by the King and by the Lacedaemonians and their allies. It shall not be lawful to make peace with the Athenians unless both agree, the King on his side and the Lacedaemonians and their allies on theirs.

3. If any revolt from the King, they shall be the enemies of the Lacedaemonians and their allies. And if any revolt from the Lacedaemonians and their allies, they shall likewise be the enemies of the King.

This was the alliance. After this the Chians immediately manned ten more vessels and sailed for Anaia, to gain intelligence of those in Miletus and also to make the cities revolt. But a message reached them from Chalcideus telling them to go back, and saying that Amorges was at hand with an army by land. They sailed to the temple of Zeus, and there they sighted ten more ships sailing up, which Diomedon had brought from Athens after Thrasycles. They fled, one ship to Ephesus and the rest to Teos. The Athenians took four of their ships empty, the men having found time to escape ashore. The rest took refuge in the city of the Teians, and the Athenians then sailed off to Samos. The Chians put to sea with their remaining vessels, accompanied by the land forces, and caused Lebedos to revolt, and after it Erae. After this the fleet and the army both returned home.

About the same time the twenty ships of the Peloponnesians in Spiraeum, which we left chased to land and blockaded by an equal number of Athenians, suddenly sallied out and defeated the blockading squadron. They took four of its ships and sailed back to Cenchreae, where they prepared again for the voyage to Chios and Ionia. Here they were joined by Astyochus, who came from Lacedaemon as high admiral and was henceforth invested with the supreme command at sea. The land forces now withdrew from Teos, and Tissaphernes went there in person with an army, completed the demolition of whatever was left of the wall, and departed. Not long after his departure Diomedon arrived with ten Athenian ships. He made an agreement by which the Teians admitted him as they had admitted the enemy, and coasted along to Erae. He failed in an attempt on the town and sailed back again.

About this time the commons at Samos rose against the upper classes, in concert with some Athenians who were there in three vessels. The Samian commons put to death some two hundred of the upper classes in all and banished four hundred more, and took their land and houses for themselves. After this the Athenians decreed the independence of the Samians, now being sure of their fidelity. The commons henceforth governed the city, excluding the landholders from all share in affairs and forbidding any of the commons to give his daughter in marriage to them or to take a wife from them in future.

After this, during the same summer, the Chians continued as active in their zeal as ever. Even without the Peloponnesians they found themselves strong enough to bring about the revolt of the cities, and they also wished to have as many companions in peril as possible. They made an expedition to Lesbos with thirteen ships of their own, since the instructions from Lacedaemon were to go to that island next and from there to the Hellespont. Meanwhile the land forces of the Peloponnesians who were with the Chians, and of the allies on the spot, moved along the coast toward Clazomenae and Cuma, under the command of Eualas, a Spartan. The fleet, under Diniadas, one of the Perioeci, first sailed up to Methymna and caused it to revolt. Leaving four ships there, he procured the revolt of Mitylene with the rest.

In the meantime Astyochus, the Lacedaemonian admiral, set sail from Cenchreae with four ships, as he had intended, and arrived at Chios. On the third day after his arrival, the Athenian ships, twenty-five in number, sailed to Lesbos under Diomedon and Leon, who had lately arrived from Athens with a reinforcement of ten ships. Late the same day Astyochus put to sea, took one Chian vessel with him, and sailed to Lesbos to give what help he could. He arrived at Pyrrha, and the next day at Eresus, where he learned that Mitylene had been taken almost without a blow by the Athenians. They had sailed up, put into the harbor unexpectedly, beaten the Chian ships, landed, and defeated the troops opposed to them, and so had become masters of the city. The Eresians told him this, and so did the Chian ships that had been left with Eubulus at Methymna and had fled when Mitylene was captured. He now fell in with three of these, one having been taken by the Athenians. Astyochus did not go on to Mitylene. He raised and armed Eresus and sent the heavy infantry from his own ships by land, under Eteonicus, to Antissa and Methymna. He himself proceeded along the coast to the same place with the ships he had with him and the three Chians, hoping that the Methymnians, on seeing them, would be encouraged to persevere in their revolt. But everything went against him in Lesbos, so he took up his own force and sailed back to Chios. The land forces on board, which were to have gone to the Hellespont, were also conveyed back to their different cities. After this six of the allied Peloponnesian ships at Cenchreae joined the forces at Chios. The Athenians restored matters in Lesbos to their old state, and set sail from there. They took Polichna, the place the Clazomenians were fortifying on the continent, and carried the inhabitants back to their town on the island, except the authors of the revolt, who withdrew to Daphnus. And so Clazomenae became Athenian once more.

The same summer the Athenians in the twenty ships at Lade, blockading Miletus, made a descent at Panormus in the Milesian territory. They killed Chalcideus the Lacedaemonian commander, who had come against them with a few men, and on the third day afterwards sailed over and set up a trophy. As they were not masters of the country, however, the Milesians pulled it down. Meanwhile Leon and Diomedon, with the Athenian fleet from Lesbos, carried on the war against the Chians from their ships. They issued from the Oenussae, the isles off Chios, from their forts of Sidussa and Pteleum in the Erythraeid, and from Lesbos, and they had on board heavy infantry from the rolls, pressed to serve as marines. They landed at Cardamyle and at Bolissus and defeated with heavy loss the Chians who took the field against them. They laid waste the places in that neighborhood, and defeated the Chians again in another battle at Phanae, and in a third at Leuconium. After this the Chians ceased to meet them in the field, and the Athenians devastated the country, which was beautifully stocked and had remained uninjured ever since the Median wars. Indeed, after the Lacedaemonians, the Chians are the only people I have known who knew how to be wise in prosperity, and who ordered their city the more securely the greater it grew. Nor did they venture on this revolt, in which they might seem to have erred on the side of rashness, until they had numerous and gallant allies to share the danger with them, and until they saw that even the Athenians, after the Sicilian disaster, no longer denied the thoroughly desperate state of their affairs. And if they were thrown out by one of the surprises that upset human calculations, they found out their mistake in company with many others who believed, as they did, in the speedy collapse of the Athenian power. While they were thus blockaded from the sea and plundered by land, some of the citizens undertook to bring the city over to the Athenians. The authorities were informed of this and took no action themselves. Instead they brought Astyochus, the admiral, from Erythrae, with the four ships he had with him, and considered how they could most quietly put an end to the conspiracy, either by taking hostages or by some other means.

While the Chians were busy with this, toward the end of the same summer a force sailed from Athens in forty-eight ships, some of them transports. It consisted of a thousand Athenian heavy infantry, fifteen hundred Argives (five hundred of them light troops equipped with armor by the Athenians) and a thousand men from the allies. Phrynichus, Onomacles and Scironides commanded it. It put in at Samos, crossed over, and encamped at Miletus. The Milesians then came out against the Athenians and their allies, with eight hundred heavy infantry, the Peloponnesians who had arrived with Chalcideus, some foreign mercenaries of Tissaphernes, and Tissaphernes himself with his cavalry. The Argives, on their own wing, charged forward with the careless disdain of men advancing against Ionians who would never withstand their attack, and the Milesians defeated them, killing little short of three hundred. The Athenians, for their part, first defeated the Peloponnesians and drove the barbarians and the rabble of the army before them. They did not engage the Milesians, who had seen the Argives routed and retreated into the town. The Athenians then crowned their victory by grounding their arms right under the walls of Miletus. So in this battle the Ionians on both sides overcame the Dorians: the Athenians beat the Peloponnesians opposed to them, and the Milesians beat the Argives. After setting up a trophy, the Athenians prepared to build a wall around the town, which stood on an isthmus. They thought that if they gained Miletus, the other towns would easily come over to them.

Meanwhile, about dusk, word reached them that fifty-five ships from Peloponnese and Sicily might be expected at any moment. Twenty-two of these came from the Siceliots, who had been urged chiefly by the Syracusan Hermocrates to help give the finishing blow to the power of Athens: twenty from Syracuse and two from Selinus. The ships we left preparing in Peloponnese were now ready, and both squadrons had been placed under Therimenes, a Lacedaemonian, to take to Astyochus, the admiral. They first put in at Leros, the island off Miletus. From there they learned that the Athenians were before the town, and they sailed into the Iasic Gulf to find out how things stood at Miletus. Meanwhile Alcibiades rode on horseback to Teichiussa in Milesian territory, the point of the gulf where they had put in for the night. He told them about the battle, in which he had fought in person beside the Milesians and Tissaphernes, and advised them, if they did not want to sacrifice Ionia and their cause, to hurry to the relief of Miletus and prevent its investment.

They therefore resolved to relieve it the next morning. Meanwhile Phrynichus, the Athenian commander, had received precise intelligence about the fleet from Leros. His colleagues wished to hold the sea and fight it out, but he flatly refused to stay himself, and refused to let them or anyone else stay if he could prevent it. He would never, he said, let the fear of a reproach of disgrace drive him into an unreasonable risk, when later they could fight after full and undisturbed preparation, knowing exactly the number of the enemy’s ships and the force they could set against them. It was no disgrace for an Athenian fleet to retreat when that suited them. However they put it, it would be more disgraceful to be beaten, and to expose the city not only to disgrace but to the most serious danger. After its recent misfortunes the city could hardly be justified in taking the offensive voluntarily, even with its strongest force, except in a case of absolute necessity. Much less, then, should it rush into a peril of its own seeking when nothing compelled it. He told them to take up their wounded as quickly as they could, along with the troops and the stores they had brought, and to leave behind what they had taken from the enemy’s country, so as to lighten the ships. Then they were to sail off to Samos, concentrate all their ships there, and attack as opportunity served. As he spoke, so he acted. In this, as afterwards, and not in this alone but in everything he had to deal with, Phrynichus showed himself a man of sense. So that very evening the Athenians broke camp before Miletus and left their victory unfinished, and the Argives, mortified at their defeat, promptly sailed home from Samos.

As soon as it was morning the Peloponnesians weighed anchor at Teichiussa and put into Miletus, after the Athenians had left. They stayed one day. On the next they took with them the Chian vessels that had originally been chased into port with Chalcideus, and resolved to sail back for the tackle they had put ashore at Teichiussa. When they arrived, Tissaphernes came to them with his land forces and persuaded them to sail against Iasus, which was held by his enemy Amorges. They attacked suddenly and took Iasus, whose inhabitants never imagined that the ships could be anything but Athenian. The Syracusans distinguished themselves most in the action. Amorges, a bastard son of Pissuthnes and a rebel against the King, was taken alive and handed over to Tissaphernes, to take to the King if he chose, as he had been ordered. The army sacked Iasus and found very great booty there, since the place had been wealthy from ancient times. The mercenaries who had served with Amorges the Peloponnesians received and enrolled in their own army without harming them, since most of them came from Peloponnese. They handed the town over to Tissaphernes with all the captives, slave or free, at the agreed price of one Doric stater a head, and then returned to Miletus. Pedaritus, son of Leon, whom the Lacedaemonians had sent to take command at Chios, they dispatched by land as far as Erythrae, with the mercenaries taken from Amorges. They appointed Philip to stay on as governor of Miletus.

Summer was now over. The winter following, Tissaphernes put Iasus in a state of defense and went on to Miletus. There he distributed a month’s pay to all the ships, as he had promised at Lacedaemon, at the rate of an Attic drachma a day for each man. In future, however, he was resolved to give no more than three obols until he had consulted the King. If the King so ordered, he said, he would then give the full drachma. But the Syracusan general Hermocrates protested. (Therimenes was not admiral but only accompanied the ships in order to hand them over to Astyochus, and so he made little difficulty about the pay.) It was agreed that, over and above the three obols a day for each man, the pay of five ships should be given in addition. Tissaphernes was to pay thirty talents a month for fifty-five ships, and for any ships beyond that number, at the same rate.

The same winter the Athenians at Samos were joined by thirty-five more vessels from home under Charminus, Strombichides and Euctemon. They called in their squadron at Chios and all the rest, intending to blockade Miletus with their navy and to send a fleet and an army against Chios, and they drew lots for the respective services. They carried out this plan. Strombichides, Onomacles and Euctemon, to whom Chios fell by lot, sailed against it with thirty ships and a part of the thousand heavy infantry who had been at Miletus, carried in transports. The rest stayed at Samos with seventy-four ships, held command of the sea, and advanced on Miletus.

Meanwhile Astyochus, whom we left at Chios collecting the hostages required because of the conspiracy, stopped when he learned that the fleet with Therimenes had arrived and that the affairs of the league were in a better condition. He put to sea with ten Peloponnesian and as many Chian vessels. After a futile attack on Pteleum he coasted on to Clazomenae, and ordered the Athenian party there to move inland to Daphnus and join the Peloponnesians. Tamos, the king’s lieutenant in Ionia, joined in giving this order. It was disregarded, and Astyochus attacked the town, which was unwalled. He failed to take it, and a strong gale carried him off to Phocaea and Cuma, while the rest of the ships put in at the islands next to Clazomenae: Marathussa, Pele and Drymussa. The winds held them there for eight days. During that time they plundered and consumed all the property of the Clazomenians deposited there, put the rest on shipboard, and sailed off to Phocaea and Cuma to join Astyochus.

While he was there, envoys came from the Lesbians, who wished to revolt again. With Astyochus they succeeded, but the Corinthians and the other allies were against it because of their earlier failure. He therefore weighed anchor and set sail for Chios, where the ships eventually arrived from different directions, a storm having scattered the fleet. After this Pedaritus, whom we left marching along the coast from Miletus, reached Erythrae, and from there crossed over to Chios with his army. There he found also about five hundred soldiers, left behind with their arms by Chalcideus from the five ships. Meanwhile some Lesbians were making offers to revolt, and Astyochus urged Pedaritus and the Chians to go with their ships and bring about the revolt of Lesbos. In that way, he said, they would increase the number of their allies, or, if they failed, at all events harm the Athenians. The Chians, however, turned a deaf ear to this, and Pedaritus flatly refused to give up the Chian vessels to him.

Upon this Astyochus took five Corinthian vessels, one Megarian, one from Hermione, and the ships that had come with him from Laconia, and set sail for Miletus to assume his command as admiral. He told the Chians, with many threats, that he would certainly not come to help them if they should be in need. At Corycus in the Erythraeid he anchored for the night. The Athenian armament, sailing from Samos against Chios, was separated from him only by a hill, on the other side of which it anchored, so that neither saw the other. But during the night a letter arrived from Pedaritus, saying that some Erythraean prisoners, who had been set free, had come from Samos to betray Erythrae. Astyochus at once put back to Erythrae, and so just escaped meeting the Athenians. Pedaritus sailed over to join him there. They inquired into the alleged treachery and found that the whole story had been invented to secure the escape of the men from Samos. They acquitted the men of the charge and sailed away, Pedaritus to Chios and Astyochus to Miletus, as he had intended.

Meanwhile the Athenian armament, sailing around Corycus, fell in with three Chian warships off Arginus and gave immediate chase. A great storm came on, and the Chians took refuge in the harbor with difficulty. The three Athenian vessels that were furthest forward in the pursuit were wrecked and thrown up near the city of Chios, and their crews were killed or taken prisoner. The rest of the Athenian fleet took refuge in the harbor called Phoenicus, under Mount Mimas, and afterwards put into Lesbos from there and prepared for the work of fortification.

The same winter the Lacedaemonian Hippocrates sailed out from Peloponnese with ten Thurian ships under the command of Dorieus, son of Diagoras, and two other commanders, together with one Laconian and one Syracusan vessel. He arrived at Cnidus, which had already revolted at the instigation of Tissaphernes. When their arrival was known at Miletus, orders came that they should leave half of their squadron to guard Cnidus, and with the rest cruise around Triopium and seize all the merchant ships arriving from Egypt. Triopium is a promontory of Cnidus, sacred to Apollo. The Athenians learned of this, sailed from Samos, and captured the six ships on watch at Triopium, though the crews escaped from them. After this the Athenians sailed into Cnidus and attacked the town, which was unfortified, and all but took it. The next day they attacked again, but with less effect, since the inhabitants had strengthened their defenses during the night and had been reinforced by the crews who had escaped from the ships at Triopium. The Athenians now withdrew, and after plundering Cnidian territory sailed back to Samos.

About the same time Astyochus came to the fleet at Miletus. The Peloponnesian camp was still plentifully supplied: it received sufficient pay, and the soldiers still had in hand the large booty taken at Iasus. The Milesians also showed great ardor for the war. Nevertheless the Peloponnesians thought the first convention with Tissaphernes, the one made with Chalcideus, defective and more advantageous to him than to them. While Therimenes was still there, they therefore concluded another, which was as follows:
The convention of the Lacedaemonians and the allies with King Darius and the sons of the King, and with Tissaphernes, for a treaty and friendship, as follows:

1. Neither the Lacedaemonians nor the allies of the Lacedaemonians shall make war against, or otherwise injure, any country or cities that belong to King Darius, or belonged to his father or to his ancestors. Neither shall the Lacedaemonians nor the allies of the Lacedaemonians exact tribute from such cities. Neither shall King Darius nor any of the subjects of the King make war against, or otherwise injure, the Lacedaemonians or their allies.
2. If the Lacedaemonians or their allies should need any assistance from the King, or the King from the Lacedaemonians or their allies, whatever they both agree upon they shall be right in doing.
3. Both shall carry on the war against the Athenians and their allies jointly; and if they make peace, both shall do so jointly.
4. The expense of all troops in the King’s country, sent for by the King, shall be borne by the King.

5. If any of the states included in this convention with the King attack the King’s country, the rest shall stop them and aid the King to the best of their power. And if anyone in the King’s country, or in the countries under the King’s rule, attacks the country of the Lacedaemonians or their allies, the King shall stop it and help them to the best of his power.

After this convention Therimenes handed over the fleet to Astyochus, sailed off in a small boat, and was lost. The Athenian armament had now crossed over from Lesbos to Chios. Being master by sea and land, it began to fortify Delphinium, a place naturally strong on the land side, with more than one harbor, and not far from the city of Chios. Meanwhile the Chians remained inactive. They had already been defeated in so many battles, and they were now also at discord among themselves. Pedaritus had executed the party of Tydeus, son of Ion, on the charge of Atticism, and had then forcibly imposed an oligarchy on the rest of the city, and this had made them suspicious of one another. They therefore thought that neither they themselves nor the mercenaries under Pedaritus were a match for the enemy. They sent, however, to Miletus to beg Astyochus to help them. He refused, and Pedaritus accordingly denounced him at Lacedaemon as a traitor. Such was the state of the Athenian affairs at Chios. Their fleet at Samos, meanwhile, kept sailing out against the enemy at Miletus, until they found that he would not accept their challenge. Then they retired again to Samos and remained quiet.

In the same winter the twenty-seven ships that the Lacedaemonians had equipped for Pharnabazus, through the agency of the Megarian Calligeitus and the Cyzicene Timagoras, put out from Peloponnese and sailed for Ionia about the time of the solstice, under the command of Antisthenes, a Spartan. With them the Lacedaemonians also sent eleven Spartans as advisers to Astyochus, among them Lichas, son of Arcesilaus. Their orders, once they arrived at Miletus, were to help generally in overseeing the good conduct of the war. They were to send these ships, or a greater or smaller number, to the Hellespont to Pharnabazus if they thought proper, appointing Clearchus, son of Ramphias, who sailed with them, to the command. They were also, if they thought proper, to make Antisthenes admiral and dismiss Astyochus, whom the letters of Pedaritus had caused to be regarded with suspicion. Sailing from Malea across the open sea, the squadron touched at Melos and there fell in with ten Athenian ships, three of which they took empty and burned. After this they feared that the Athenian vessels that had escaped from Melos might report their approach to the Athenians at Samos, as in fact they did. They therefore sailed to Crete and, having lengthened their voyage as a precaution, made land at Caunus in Asia. From there, thinking themselves safe, they sent a message to the fleet at Miletus asking for a convoy along the coast.

Meanwhile the Chians and Pedaritus, undeterred by the backwardness of Astyochus, kept sending messengers to press him to come with the whole fleet to help them against their besiegers, and not to leave the greatest of the allied states in Ionia shut up by sea and overrun and pillaged by land. There were more slaves at Chios than in any other city except Lacedaemon, and because of their numbers they were also punished more severely when they offended. So when most of them saw the Athenian armament firmly established on the island with a fortified position, they immediately deserted to the enemy, and through their knowledge of the country did the greatest mischief. The Chians therefore urged Astyochus that it was his duty to help them, while there was still hope and a possibility of stopping the enemy’s progress: Delphinium was still being fortified and was unfinished, and the higher rampart being added to protect the camp and fleet of their besiegers was not yet complete. Astyochus now saw that the allies also wished it, and prepared to go, in spite of his intention to the contrary because of the threat already mentioned.

In the meantime news came from Caunus that the twenty-seven ships had arrived with the Lacedaemonian commissioners. Astyochus put everything else second to the duty of convoying a fleet of that importance, so as to be better able to command the sea, and to the safe conduct of the Lacedaemonians who had been sent to spy on his behavior. He at once gave up going to Chios and set sail for Caunus. As he coasted along he landed at the Meropid Cos and sacked the city, which was unfortified and had recently been laid in ruins by an earthquake, by far the greatest in living memory. The inhabitants had fled to the mountains, so he overran the country and took as booty all it contained, letting the free men go, however. From Cos he arrived in the night at Cnidus. There the representations of the Cnidians constrained him not to disembark the sailors but to sail straight on as he was against the twenty Athenian vessels. These were on watch, with Charminus, one of the commanders at Samos, for the very twenty-seven ships from Peloponnese that Astyochus himself was sailing to join. The Athenians at Samos had heard from Melos of their approach, and Charminus, who now heard that they were at Caunus, was keeping a lookout off Syme, Chalce, Rhodes and Lycia.

Astyochus accordingly sailed as he was to Syme, before he was heard of, hoping to catch the enemy somewhere out at sea. But he met rain and foggy weather, which made his ships straggle and fall into disorder in the dark. In the morning his fleet had separated and was for the most part still straggling around the island, and only the left wing was in sight of Charminus and the Athenians. They took it for the squadron they were watching for from Caunus and hastily put out against it with only part of their twenty vessels. They attacked immediately, sank three ships and disabled others, and had the advantage in the action until the main body of the fleet unexpectedly came into sight and they were surrounded on every side. They then took to flight, and after losing six ships escaped with the rest to Teutlussa or Beet Island, and from there to Halicarnassus. After this the Peloponnesians put into Cnidus and, joined by the twenty-seven ships from Caunus, sailed out all together and set up a trophy at Syme, and then returned to anchor at Cnidus.

As soon as the Athenians knew of the sea-fight, they sailed with all the ships at Samos to Syme. Without attacking the fleet at Cnidus or being attacked by it, they took the ships’ tackle left at Syme, touched at Lorymi on the mainland, and sailed back to Samos. Meanwhile the Peloponnesian ships, now all at Cnidus, underwent the repairs they needed. The eleven Lacedaemonian commissioners conferred with Tissaphernes, who had come to meet them, about the points that did not satisfy them in the past transactions, and about the best and most mutually advantageous way of conducting the war in future. The severest critic of the present proceedings was Lichas. He said that neither of the treaties could stand, neither that of Chalcideus nor that of Therimenes. It was monstrous, he said, that the King should at this date claim possession of all the country formerly ruled by himself or by his ancestors. That claim implicitly put all the islands back under the yoke, with Thessaly, Locris and everything as far as Boeotia, and it made the Lacedaemonians give the Hellenes a Median master instead of liberty. He therefore invited Tissaphernes to conclude another and a better treaty, since they certainly would not recognize those existing, and did not want any of his pay on such conditions. This offended Tissaphernes so much that he went away in a rage without settling anything.
